stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: An astable multivibrator has no stable state — it flips itself. The two collectors produce complementary square waves at $f = 1/T$ with $T = 2\,R\,C\,\ln 2$. Sweep $R$ to change the period. Reach both a low-frequency setting ($f < 400\,\text{Hz}$) and a high-frequency setting ($f > 1500\,\text{Hz}$) to advance.
stages.concept: The two RC coupling networks each set a half-period $t = R\,C\,\ln 2$. With symmetric $R_1 = R_2 = R$ and $C_1 = C_2 = C$: $T = 2\,R\,C\,\ln 2 \approx 1.386\,R\,C$. Halving $R$ or $C$ doubles the frequency. No sine, no external drive — the circuit oscillates on its own.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: The target frequency is shown as an orange line on the scope. Move the $R$ slider until your green square wave matches the target within $\pm 10\%$. Watch the frequency readout at the top-right.
stages.concept: $f = \dfrac{1}{2\,R\,C\,\ln 2}$. To tune from a starting frequency $f_0$ to a target $f_t$, scale $R$ by $f_0 / f_t$. Larger $R$ → longer period → lower frequency.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: The scope shows a target waveform (orange). Identify the circuit variant that produces it — a plain symmetric astable, or an astable followed by an integrator. Compute on paper first, then SUBMIT. Wrong answers restart the deck.
stages.concept: Symmetric 2-transistor astable → square wave (each output alternates between $0$ and $V_{CC}$). Feed that square into an op-amp integrator ($V_{out} = -\frac{1}{RC}\int V_{in}\,dt$) → a linear ramp on each half-period, i.e. a triangular wave. Shape reveals topology.

labels.tip1: sweep R · see how frequency scales with 1 / (R C)
labels.tip2: match the target f · slide R until the green trace lines up
labels.tip3: compute the shape on paper · then SUBMIT
labels.peek_tip_1: Square wave → symmetric astable alone. Triangular → an integrator after the astable turns each half-period into a linear ramp.
labels.peek_tip_2: Frequency: f = 1 / (1.386 R C). Halve R to double the frequency. Shape is set by the topology, not R or C.

1.1: Move R to the extreme ends of its range. Watch how the period T on the scope grows and shrinks.
1.2: T = 2 R C ln 2. Bigger R → longer T → lower f. With C fixed at 33 nF, R = 10 kΩ gives f ≈ 2.2 kHz; R = 100 kΩ gives f ≈ 218 Hz.
1.3: You need one setting with f < 400 Hz AND one with f > 1500 Hz. Try R near the max, then R near the min.

2.1: The orange trace is the target period. Your green trace must line up with it in time.
2.2: Target f is written next to the target trace. Read your current f in the HUD and slide R until they match (±10%).
2.3: If your f is too low, decrease R. If too high, increase R. f is inversely proportional to R.

3.1: There is no help trace. Look at the target shape only. Square? Triangular?
3.2: A pure astable can only make square waves. Anything with linear ramps needs an integrator downstream.
3.3: Square wave = symmetric astable. Triangular wave = astable + integrator. Wrong SUBMIT restarts the deck.
